sections.html:
Manchester sits on the Merrimack River in south-central New Hampshire, about 20 miles from the Massachusetts border and 58 miles from Boston. The city is in Hillsborough County, which shares its county seat role between Manchester and Nashua, and it had 115,644 residents in 2020. Many buyers commute to Boston or Concord. About half of occupied homes are rented, which means a sale often involves tenants, or a landlord with more than one property.

The city's 2010 Master Plan divides it into 25 neighborhoods, and assessments and house styles change a lot from one to the next.

  • West Side: Amoskeag, Rimmon Heights, Notre Dame/McGregorville, and Piscataquog/Granite Square
  • East Side: North End, Janeville/Corey Square, Hallsville, and Bakersville
  • Outer areas: Youngsville and Goffes Falls

A West Side seller and a Goffes Falls seller deal with the same Board of Assessors and Tax Collector, but the buyer pool and the age of the housing can look very different.

The mills defined Manchester for a century after it incorporated as a city in 1846, so the housing stock is older than most. An older house is more likely to need work before it shows well.

  • Older roofs and chimneys take freeze and thaw cycles every year.
  • Heating systems in 1960s houses are often original or near the end of their life.
  • Homes near the Merrimack, the Piscataquog or Cohas Brook deserve a look at the basement and the flood zone status before listing.

A cash offer already reflects those items, and that is why many owners with deferred repairs go with an as-is sale.

Each Manchester tax year runs from April 1 to March 31 (RSA 76:2) and reflects the inventory taken in April. Value comes from the Board of Assessors, and the bill comes from the Office of the Tax Collector.

Assessors reach value three ways: recent sales of comparable properties, replacement cost less depreciation, and, for income property such as apartments, an income approach. Dividing the levy by total assessed value gives the rate, which is the same for every owner. The state Department of Revenue Administration issues it in October or November.

Two bills arrive each year. The early June bill uses half of the previous year's rate. The late November bill uses the new rate and any assessment changes. Payment is due 30 days after issue. The 2025 rate is 20.24 per $1,000, up from 19.58 for 2024, and a separate Central Business Service District rate of 0.462730 applies for 2025.

Unpaid tax moves from interest to a lien in about a year and can end in a city tax deed after two years.

StepWhat happens
Interest8 percent per year on late taxes (RSA 76:13)
Notice of ArrearageSent about 30 days after each billing (RSA 76:11-b)
Notice of Impending LienCertified mail at least 30 days before the lien is executed (RSA 80:60)
Lien executedInterest becomes 14 percent per year (RSA 80:69); lien recorded at the Registry of Deeds within 30 days
Mortgagee noticeSent 60 days after execution, with a $10 fee plus any title search cost (RSA 80:67)
Tax deedIf unpaid two years after execution, with a notice of impending deed at least 30 days earlier (RSA 80:76, 80:77)

A former owner or mortgagee who wants the property back after a deed must tell the city by certified mail within 30 days of the notice of intent to repurchase, and must prove they can cover back taxes, interest, costs and a 10 percent penalty on the equalized assessed value (RSA 80:89).

Your abatement application goes to the Board of Assessors in writing, received or postmarked by March 1 after the final tax bill. Filing online is not allowed because an original signature is required, and the city charges no fee.

The applicant must have owned the property on April 1 of the tax year, or be otherwise aggrieved, and must show the property was assessed out of proportion to other property in town. The Board decides by July 1. Silence by then counts as a denial.

  • A further appeal is due by September 1.
  • Pick one route: the State Board of Tax and Land Appeals (written, with a fee) or Hillsborough County Superior Court, Northern District, 300 Chestnut Street, Manchester.
  • Going to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals gives up the right to petition the Superior Court (RSA 76-B:11).

If you are selling and think the value is wrong, tell the title company about the pending application, because the result affects the tax bill for the year you owned the house.

Give the title company a heads-up at the very start. Unpaid tax and any recorded lien come out of your sale proceeds at closing. The Tax Collector will provide a copy of a lien release for $10 per property plus $2 per receipt requested, by email at Taxcollector@manchesternh.gov or in person at One City Hall Plaza.

A redeemed lien is released within 30 days, and the release is mailed to the Hillsborough County Register of Deeds, 19 Temple Street, Nashua. Deeds can take 30 days or longer to reach the Assessors, which means a bill may still carry your name after closing. Send the new owner's name and address along in writing.

The state's transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price, with buyer and seller each paying and a $20 minimum each at prices of $4,000 or less. You buy the stamps from the register of deeds. Within 30 days after the deed is recorded, the state expects the Purchaser's and Seller's Declarations of Consideration (CD-57-P and CD-57-S) and the PA-34 inventory.

sections.h2: What buyers will ask about a Manchester house
sections.html: Neighborhood matters here. A buyer looking at the West Side, the East Side or Goffes Falls will have different expectations for age and condition. Be ready to say how old the roof and heating system are, whether the basement has ever taken on water, and whether the house sits near the river or the brook. A seller who answers those questions before they are asked usually keeps the deal on track.

With about half of occupied homes rented, many Manchester sellers are landlords. If your property has tenants, gather the leases, deposit records and rent roll before you talk to a buyer. Find out whether the building is near the river, the Piscataquog or Cohas Brook, since flood status is a common question. A cash buyer can take over a tenant-occupied building as is, but the lease terms still decide how quickly the buyer can use the property.

faqs.q: When is Manchester property tax due?
faqs.a: Two bills a year, each due 30 days after issue. The first is mailed in early June and the second in late November, and the tax year runs April 1 to March 31.

faqs.q: What is the interest rate on late Manchester property tax?
faqs.a: 8 percent per year on unpaid taxes under RSA 76:13. Once a tax lien is executed, interest on the lien is 14 percent per year under RSA 80:69.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Manchester house if there is a tax lien on it?
faqs.a: Yes. The lien is paid from the sale proceeds and released after payment, and a full redemption leads to a release within 30 days. Ask the Tax Collector for the current payoff before closing.

faqs.q: Who pays the New Hampshire transfer tax when a house sells?
faqs.a: Both do. Each of the buyer and the seller pays $0.75 per $100 of the price, and transfers by will or intestate succession are exempt.

faqs.q: Where do I appeal a Manchester assessment after the Board of Assessors denies it?
faqs.a: File by September 1 with either the State Board of Tax and Land Appeals or Hillsborough County Superior Court, Northern District. You pick one, and choosing the state board waives the court option.
